title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 4
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Material That Does Not Last
passages.text:
A. Concrete is the most used manufactured substance on earth, and the assumption embedded in most of its use is that it is permanent. Structures are designed, financed and insured on the basis of a service life measured in many decades. The assumption is reasonable for the material as a whole and wrong in a specific and expensive way, because what fails is usually not the concrete.

B. Modern structural concrete contains steel reinforcement, and the two materials are combined because their weaknesses are complementary: concrete resists compression and fails under tension, while steel does the reverse. The pairing also works chemically. Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, and that alkalinity forms a passive layer on the steel which prevents it from rusting. For as long as that chemistry holds, the reinforcement is protected by the material surrounding it.

C. The chemistry does not hold indefinitely. Carbon dioxide from the air penetrates the concrete slowly and neutralises the alkalinity, a process called carbonation that advances from the surface inward at a rate depending on the density of the mix. Chloride, from seawater or from salt applied to roads in winter, attacks the passive layer directly and far faster. When either reaches the steel, corrosion begins — and rust occupies substantially more volume than the metal it replaces, so the reinforcement expands and cracks the concrete from within. The visible spalling is the last stage, not the first.

D. Roman concrete is frequently invoked as evidence that the modern material is inferior, and the comparison is misleading in a way worth stating plainly. Roman structures survive partly because they were unreinforced: with no steel inside, there was nothing to corrode. They were also built in compression, in massive sections, using a volcanic ash mix whose chemistry continues reacting with seawater over centuries. Modern reinforced concrete does something Roman concrete cannot — it spans, it cantilevers, it carries tension — and the durability cost is a consequence of that capability rather than of carelessness.

E. Repair is where the economics become difficult. Diagnosis requires investigation that is expensive relative to the value of the information, so deterioration is typically identified when it becomes visible, by which point the internal damage is advanced. A structure can be structurally sound and simultaneously past the point where surface repair will arrest the process, and the choice at that stage is between an intervention costing a substantial share of replacement value and a managed decline.

F. What follows is a design argument rather than a materials one. Extending service life depends less on stronger concrete than on keeping the aggressive agents away from the steel: adequate cover depth, dense low-permeability mixes, drainage that removes standing water, and detailing that prevents salt-laden runoff tracking across surfaces. These are unglamorous decisions made early, at low cost, by people who will not be present when the consequences arrive.

passages.title: The Price of Water
passages.text:
Water is unusual among essential commodities in that its price almost nowhere reflects its scarcity. In most systems, households pay a tariff set to recover the cost of treatment and distribution, and agriculture — which accounts for the large majority of consumption globally — frequently pays a fraction of that or nothing at all. The result is that the sector using most of the resource faces the weakest signal to use less of it.

Economists have argued for decades that pricing water closer to its scarcity value would reduce waste more efficiently than any regulation, and the theoretical case is strong. The practical objections are also strong, and they are not the ones usually raised. The common objection, that water is a human right and should not be sold, is answerable: a right to a basic quantity is compatible with charging for consumption above it, and several systems do exactly that with a free or heavily subsidised initial block.

The harder objection concerns measurement. Charging by volume requires metering, and in agriculture, where the gains would be largest, the water is frequently drawn from groundwater by private wells that no authority monitors. Where abstraction cannot be measured it cannot be priced, and where thousands of individual wells draw on a shared aquifer, each user's restraint benefits everyone while its cost falls on them alone — a structure that reliably produces depletion regardless of what the law says.

Subsidy also proves harder to remove than to criticise. Agricultural water pricing is typically low because it was set when policy sought to secure domestic food production, and it has been capitalised into land values ever since. Raising it does not simply change a cost; it reduces the value of an asset that farmers have borrowed against. This is why reform proposals that are analytically sound fail politically with a consistency that surprises their authors.

There is also a distributional pattern that the theory handles badly. Where prices rise, consumption falls most among those least able to pay, which is efficient in the narrow sense and produces outcomes most societies reject. Systems that have raised prices successfully have generally paired the increase with a rising block structure and explicit protection for low-income households — measures that reduce the efficiency gain and are the condition of it being politically survivable.

The most effective interventions have often not been price at all. Requiring efficient irrigation technology, licensing abstraction with enforceable caps, and repairing distribution networks that lose a substantial share of treated water before it reaches anyone have each delivered measurable savings in systems where price reform stalled. That these are less elegant than a market-clearing price is not an argument against them.

passages.title: Finding the Way Without a Map
passages.text:
Animals that travel long distances and arrive accurately have been studied for over a century, and the accumulated explanation is not one mechanism but several, used in combination and switched between according to conditions.

The simplest is path integration: an animal tracks its own movement, continuously updating an estimate of the direct route home. Desert ants demonstrate it cleanly. Having wandered a foraging path of many turns, an ant on finding food runs almost straight back toward the nest, and if displaced experimentally it runs the vector it had computed rather than toward the nest's actual position — which shows the calculation is internal and not a response to the destination. Path integration accumulates error, so it works well over short distances and requires correction over long ones.

Celestial cues supply that correction. Many species use the sun's position with a clock-based compensation for its movement, and the compensation can be demonstrated by shifting an animal's internal clock: an animal held under artificial light cycles departs at a predictable angle to the correct direction. Nocturnal migrants use star patterns, and experiments in planetariums established that some birds orient to the centre of rotation of the night sky rather than to individual constellations, which is a more robust cue because it does not change across seasons.

Magnetic sensing is the best-evidenced and least understood. That birds, turtles and some insects respond to magnetic fields is not in serious dispute; the receptor has been harder to identify than the behaviour. Two candidate mechanisms are debated — magnetite particles acting mechanically, and a light-dependent chemical reaction in the eye — and evidence exists for both, in different species and sometimes in the same one. The field's honest position is that the behaviour is established and the physiology is not settled.

Olfactory information matters more than was long assumed, particularly at the final stage. Homing pigeons made anosmic navigate poorly from unfamiliar release sites while performing normally over known ground, which suggests smell contributes to determining position rather than to holding a heading. The finding was resisted for years, partly because a map made of odours is difficult to imagine and partly because the early experiments were genuinely confounded.

What emerges is redundancy rather than elegance. An animal deprived of one cue usually compensates with another, and performance degrades gradually rather than failing, which is why single-cue experiments produced contradictory results for decades. It also explains why navigation is vulnerable in a way that is easy to miss: a system with several overlapping cues tolerates the loss of any one, and light pollution, magnetic disturbance and habitat change remove several at once.
